report:
**Conclusion: The claim is supported by high-quality evidence.**

The landmark randomized controlled trial directly comparing chlorhexidine–alcohol versus iodine–alcohol for preoperative skin antisepsis before cesarean delivery was published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Tuuli et al., 2016). In this trial of over 900 women, chlorhexidine–alcohol resulted in a significantly lower rate of surgical-site infection (SSI) compared with iodine–alcohol (4.0% vs. 7.3%; relative risk 0.55). This is the most directly relevant study to the claim.

A subsequent Cochrane systematic review (Hadiati et al., 2020) and a network meta-analysis (2024) both found that alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of being effective in preventing SSI after cesarean section, though some smaller trials did not reach statistical significance individually. A pilot RCT from India (2021) showed a trend favoring chlorhexidine–alcohol but was underpowered to reach significance.

Overall, the best available evidence—from the largest and most rigorous RCT as well as systematic reviews and meta-analyses—supports that chlorhexidine–alcohol skin preparation before cesarean delivery reduces surgical-site infection compared with iodine-based preparations (including iodine–alcohol). The benefit is consistent with chlorhexidine's superior residual antimicrobial activity and rapid onset of action.

**Sources:**
1. Tuuli MG et al. "A Randomized Trial Comparing Skin Antiseptic Agents at Cesarean Delivery." *NEJM*, 2016. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048
2. Hadiati DR et al. "Skin preparation for preventing infection following caesarean section." *Cochrane Database*, 2020. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32580252/
3. Network meta-analysis, *Journal of Hospital Infection*, 2024. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282
4. Pilot RCT, *PMC*, 2021. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/
